## What This Lab Is About

This isn't a gruelling lab — but it's an important one. By the end of today you need to have done three things:

::: {.callout-important}
## Today's Three Goals

1. **Form your group** (3–4 is ideal, but more or fewer is fine — the key thing is that you join a group)
2. **Choose your project topic** (from the example list, or propose your own)
3. **Find a key paper** — something to anchor your methodology, procedure, or hypothesis to
:::

That's it. Get those three things done and you're set up for the rest of the term.

## Part 1: Form Your Group

### Why This Matters

Your group will work together for the rest of the term — choosing a topic, designing a study, collecting data, and sharing results. Each person then writes their own individual Research Report (2,000 words, due mid–late April).

**Group size:** 3–4 students is ideal, but larger or smaller groups are fine. The most important thing is that **everyone joins a group**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Group Allocation
Students not part of a registered group this week will be **allocated to a group** if they emerge down the line. So please register today — even if your plans are still forming.
:::

### Register Your Group

Once you've found your people, **register your group using this form**:

::: {.callout-important}
## Group Registration Form

**[Register your group here](https://forms.office.com/Pages/ResponsePage.aspx?id=Px9DDcEgHEaVikaynU4CG8gqdkQ5QElOkXjIDHSz7DVURjBMUUo1TFNBUElCUEpGWVlZRzFSMDdYVy4u)**

Enter your group members' names and any preliminary topic ideas. You can change your topic later — the important thing is to register.
:::

### Group Setup Checklist

**Individually (after term):** Write your own 2,000-word Research Report using the group's shared data. Same data, different reports. **Do NOT share written drafts** — that's academic misconduct.

## Part 2: Choose Your Topic

### What Makes a Good Topic?

Your project needs to be:

- **Testable with a t-test** — either a between-groups comparison (independent samples) or a within-subjects comparison (repeated measures) across two conditions
- **Feasible in scale** — your group of 3–4 should be able to run ~15–20 participants in a couple of hours. Think short tasks: memorise 20 words, 2-minute distractor, 2-minute recall — that sort of size
- **Ethically straightforward** — no deception that could cause distress, no sensitive topics, nothing requiring specialist equipment

### Option 1: Choose from the Example List

I've put together **9 fully scoped project options**, all ready to go. You're welcome to pick one directly.

**[View the Project Options](https://littlemonkeylab.github.io/PS50008A_2526/project/group-project-options.html)**

Here's a quick comparison:

| Project | Topic | Domain | Expected Effect | Materials |
|---------|-------|--------|----------------|-----------|
| A | Smiling & approachability | Social | Medium–large | Low (photos + paper) |
| B | Background music & recall | Cognitive | Medium | Low (speaker + phone) |
| C | Colour & memory | Cognitive | Small–medium | Low (colour printer) |
| D | Imagery vs repetition | Cognitive | Medium–large | Very low (paper only) |
| E | Phone presence & attention | Social/Cognitive | Small–medium | Very low (own phones) |
| F | Testing effect on learning | Cognitive | Medium–large | Low (paper only) |
| G | Social facilitation | Social | Small–medium | Low (confederates) |
| H | Anchoring & estimates | Social/Cognitive | Large | Very low (paper only) |
| I | Name stereotypes & competence | Social | Small–medium | Very low (paper only) |

### Option 2: Propose Your Own

If none of the examples appeal, you can propose your own topic. You'll need to:

1. **Identify a clear IV with two levels** (e.g., music vs silence, phone visible vs hidden)
2. **Identify a measurable DV** (e.g., number of words recalled, response time, rating score)
3. **Find at least one paper** to anchor your hypothesis and methodology to
4. **Check it's ethically straightforward** — if in doubt, ask Gordon

**4. A good project topic for this module must be testable with:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Any statistical test</option><option value=''>A correlation</option><option value='answer'>A two-group t-test (between or within subjects)</option><option value=''>An ANOVA</option></select>

**5. In a between-subjects design:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>Each participant does all conditions</option><option value='answer'>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>There is no control group</option><option value=''>The IV is measured, not manipulated</option></select>

**6. In a within-subjects design:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>Each participant does all conditions</option><option value=''>Different participants are in each condition</option><option value=''>Only one condition is used</option><option value=''>The DV changes between groups</option></select>

## Part 3: Find a Key Paper

### Why You Need One

Every project needs a foundation — a paper that gives you:

- A **concept or theory** to base your hypothesis on
- An **operationalisation** you can adapt (how did they measure the DV? What stimuli did they use?)
- A **procedure** you can build from or simplify

A single well-chosen paper is more valuable than three vaguely related ones.

### Where to Look

**Starting-point papers** are available on Learn for each of the 9 example topics:

- **[Project papers folder on Learn](https://learn.gold.ac.uk/mod/folder/view.php?id=1795121)** — a couple of papers per topic. They're not all perfect, but they offer a starting point for operationalisation, background, or methodology.

These may not be the ideal paper for your specific angle — a quick literature search may turn up something better:

::: {.callout-tip}
## Quick Search Tips
- **PsycINFO** (via [Goldsmiths Library](https://www.gold.ac.uk/library/)) — psychology-specific, peer-reviewed
- **Google Scholar** (scholar.google.com) — broader coverage, citation tracking
- Start with your key variables as search terms
- Use **quotation marks** for exact phrases (e.g., `"background music" AND recall`)
:::

If your group has chosen its own topic (not from the list), finding a source paper is essential — it's what your methodology and hypothesis will be built on.

**1. When you first find a paper, you should read:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>The entire paper carefully</option><option value='answer'>The abstract first, to check relevance</option><option value=''>Only the results</option><option value=''>The reference list</option></select>

**2. The Method section of a relevant paper helps you because:**

<select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>You can copy their procedure</option><option value='answer'>It shows how similar studies have been designed and measured the DV</option><option value=''>It tells you what results to expect</option><option value=''>It's not useful for your project</option></select>

True or False: A paper published in 2010 can still be a useful source if it's highly cited and relevant. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value='answer'>TRUE</option><option value=''>FALSE</option></select>

True or False: Wikipedia is an acceptable source for your Research Report reference list. <select class='webex-select'><option value='blank'></option><option value=''>TRUE</option><option value='answer'>FALSE</option></select>
